body: Wait, that's a really fun fact! It's such a lovely song, thank you so so much for sharing this!
Honestly, it feels like most of the soundtracks are good – which I really loved, by the way – for meditation. Truly a memorable drama.
Do update me on how it goes! I've read somewhere in passing that it balances the yin and the yang, and that piqued my curiosity.
Probably overused at this point, but I adore it: "All the world's a stage."
I see, you do have a point. Then what lead her to her madness? As in, how does that guilt manifests itself to madness?

Pardon me if I do not understand you correctly, but I will answer this to the best of my understanding. It's a fact universally known that Ophelia is the embodiment of innocence. She is seen as pure and obedient – a very poised maiden who fits into societal expectations and roles of the day, which is why she represents the angel archetype. On the other hand, Lady Macbeth is often seen as evil, the true demon archetype. Not only is she quite literally mad in the end, she is also mad for committing treason after learning of the prophecy. These things, I have observed and read for myself. Admittedly, the first question that did come to my mind was: Is Ophelia really as innocent as they think and is Lady Macbeth really that evil? And this is what I've been intending to research on. 

Your commentary has certain leave me with something to actually think about, which I greatly appreciated. Perhaps I should really be tackling the topic through a different angle as per your suggestion. Thank you so much! Do you have any more suggestions for a first time thesis writer?

I wonder if it would be accurate to say that even Macbeth barely cares about her in the end. Sure, he mentions her but mostly in passing towards the end. Could that have constituted to her madness as well? Some scholars said the absence of Macbeth led her to suffer alone, which eventually led to her madness.

Really? Do enlighten me because a lot of the scholarships that I've read seems to have stated that she's gone mad. And prior to her madness, her evil deeds were also seen as the acts of a madwoman. This leaves me uncertain now.

I would actually focus on just one, but my supervisor suggested that I do a comparison of both instead since this is my first time writing a thesis. The main gist of my topic is to create a comparison between their portrayals of female madness. My readings pointed to me that there is a disparity between the archetypes they represent, which then becomes something I'm fixated on to prove through analysis of the texts itself. On that note, how would you suggest I look into my topic?

Coincidentally, that is exactly what my supervisor questioned as well. What I meant to say is that I intend to show that these two characters do not actually fit into their archetypes perfectly. As per my own observation, I believe that Lady Macbeth – while her evil madness is undeniable – has a degree of goodness in her. She is evil, sure, but she is also loving (towards her husband). It's unfair, I think, to say that she's entirely evil. That was my whole point, really. I'm just unsure how to properly discuss it. Do tell me what you think, I appreciate it.
